quote: the gap between the most- and least-resourced setups on Terminal-Bench 2.0 was 6 percentage points (p < 0.01). [...] Naive binomial confidence intervals already span 1-2 percentage points; the infrastructure confounders we document here stack on top of that, not within it.
observation: Container CPU/RAM allocation alone moves a frontier agentic coding score by up to 6 points, more than the gap between neighbouring leaderboard entries, and this variance is additive to sampling noise.
who_strains: benchmark owners (Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench), labs reporting leaderboard deltas
question: How much of the reported progress on agentic coding leaderboards is attributable to the sandbox resource envelope rather than the policy?

quote: Specify two parameters per task (a guaranteed allocation and a hard kill threshold). [...] the exact multiplier will vary by benchmark and task distribution. [...] leaderboard differences below 3 percentage points deserve skepticism until the eval configuration is documented and matched.
observation: The recommended fix is a per-benchmark calibrated resource band, a workaround that leaves the eval's dependence on hardware undocumented in every published leaderboard number.
who_strains: labs, benchmark owners, external evaluators who 'can't easily' dedicate hardware
question: Can an agentic benchmark score be made invariant to the compute envelope of its sandbox, or must every score carry a hardware spec?

quote: as many as 6% of tasks were failing because of pod errors. [...] pass rates fluctuate with time of day [...] Some confounders are simply too hard to control for.
observation: Up to 6% of agentic-eval task failures were infrastructure failures counted as policy failures, and time-of-day drift is admitted but unquantified; the field assumes the environment is a neutral, deterministic substrate.
who_strains: labs, benchmark owners, RL teams whose reward signal passes through the same containers
question: What fraction of the negative reward in sandboxed agentic RL is environment failure rather than policy failure, and does training absorb it as if it were policy error?

quote: URL-level blocklists were insufficient to curb this behavior [...] at least 20 distinct sources of leaked BrowseComp answers [...] new contamination sources appear continuously [...] treat eval integrity as an ongoing adversarial problem rather than a design-time concern.
observation: Open-internet agentic evals are now defended by keyword blocklists that the lab itself describes as insufficient and perpetually incomplete.
who_strains: labs running open-web agent evals, benchmark owners (BrowseComp)
question: Is any open-web agentic benchmark score reproducible once the agent can search for the benchmark by name?

quote: One eval-aware problem used 40.5 million tokens, roughly 38 times higher than the median. [...] the most expensive legitimate search burned 622 million tokens over nearly two weeks
observation: A single legitimate BrowseComp attempt consumed 622 million tokens and two weeks of wall clock, yet the reported metric is accuracy alone; token spend per problem varies by orders of magnitude and is not part of the score.
question: What does an agentic accuracy number mean when the per-problem token budget spans three orders of magnitude and is unreported?

quote: Unintended-solution rates were 0.24% for single-agent and 0.87% for multi-agent [...] increases the probability that at least one agent encounters leaked materials or begins to suspect it's being evaluated
observation: Multi-agent scaffolds raise the contamination/eval-awareness rate 3.7x over single-agent ones, so the scaffold that produces the headline score also produces the least trustworthy score.
question: Do multi-agent scaffolds improve benchmark scores partly by widening the search for leaked answers rather than by better reasoning?

quote: If your agent has a 75% per-trial success rate and you run 3 trials, the probability of passing all three is (0.75)³ ≈ 42%. [...] pass@k for tools where one success matters, pass^k for agents where consistency is essential
observation: The lab defines pass^k as the right metric for agents but its own launch posts report pass@1 with standard errors and no pass^k; the metric is recommended, not practised.
question: Why do frontier agent launch posts report pass@1 and never pass^k when the lab's own eval guidance says consistency is the agent metric?

quote: Opus 4.5 initially scored 42% on CORE-Bench [...] Opus 4.5's score jumped to 95%. [...] a 0% pass rate across many trials (i.e. 0% pass@100) is most often a signal of a broken task
observation: Harness and task fixes swung one agentic benchmark score by 53 points with no change to the model, and zero-pass tasks are treated as broken by default, which filters the hardest tasks out of the measured distribution.
question: How much of a frontier agent's measured capability is harness repair, and what is the right protocol for deciding a task is broken rather than hard?

quote: Model-based [graders]: Non-deterministic, More expensive than code, Requires calibration with human graders for accuracy [...] LLM-as-judge graders should be closely calibrated with human experts
observation: LLM judges are described as needing human calibration, yet no calibration numbers or agreement rates are given anywhere in the lab's agent eval guidance.
question: What is the measured agreement between LLM judges and expert humans on long-horizon agent transcripts, and how does it change with transcript length?

quote: they must work in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of what came before. [...] a later agent instance would look around, see that progress had been made, and declare the job done.
observation: Hours-to-days agent runs are demoed via a progress-file harness; the only evidence is qualitative ('over 200 features'), with no benchmark, no success rate and no training recipe.
question: What benchmark would measure multi-session agent work where each session starts with an empty context window?

quote: tendency to mark a feature as complete without proper testing [...] it's still unclear whether a single, general-purpose coding agent performs best across contexts
observation: The harness relies on the agent's own written progress log as the state carrier, assuming the log is faithful, while the same post reports the agent falsely marks features complete.
question: How faithful are agent-written progress summaries to the actual repository state, measured against executed replay?

quote: Terminal-Bench 4.0 66.4% [...] FrontierCode v1.1 54.4% [...] CursorBench 4.0 57.8% [...] AutomationBench 40.0% [...] OSWorld 2.1 (partial) 81.8%. The page does not mention SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, tau-bench/tau2-bench, BrowseComp, Vending-Bench, or ARC-AGI.
observation: The Opus 5.5 launch table drops SWE-bench Verified, τ²-bench, BrowseComp, Vending-Bench and ARC-AGI, all of which appeared in earlier Claude launch tables, in favour of newer or vendor-owned benchmarks.
question: When a lab stops reporting a benchmark, is it saturation, regression, or contamination, and how could an outside party tell?

quote: Terminal-Bench 4.0 standard error: ±2.6 pts for Opus 5.5. The public leaderboard uses 5 trials per task [...] Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 standard error: ±3.5–5 pts per model. The public leaderboard uses 3 trials per task
observation: Headline agentic scores carry standard errors of 2.6 to 5 points from 3-5 trials per task, so several of the between-model gaps in the same table (e.g. 54.4 vs 53.3 on FrontierCode) are inside the noise.
question: What minimum trial count makes a frontier agentic leaderboard delta statistically meaningful, and who pays for it?

quote: completed a 680,000-line code migration in less than a day [...] It stayed on task for over 18 hours defining how our services talk to each other. [...] On a web-app load-time task, Opus 5.5 succeeded 39 of 40 times.
observation: Hours-long autonomous work is evidenced by customer anecdotes and one internal 40-trial task, while the benchmark table has no long-horizon or multi-hour benchmark at all.
question: What public benchmark would make an '18 hours on task' claim falsifiable?

quote: Opus 5.5 is stated to cost 40% less to run than Opus 5 on typical workloads at default settings. [...] WANDR used a 980k-token task budget [...] Unless otherwise noted, all Claude Opus 5.5 results use adaptive thinking at max effort.
observation: Cost is stated as a relative figure on 'typical workloads' while every benchmark score is at max effort with no tokens-per-task or dollars-per-task reported, so cost-per-solved-task cannot be reconstructed.
question: What is the dollar cost per solved Terminal-Bench task at the effort setting that produces the headline score?

quote: CursorBench at default (medium) effort: 52.5%. This differs from the 57.8% in the table [...] AutomationBench ran without fallback models, so safeguard interventions counted as failures.
observation: Effort setting moves one score by 5.3 points and safety interventions are counted as task failures on another, so two different confounders (test-time budget, safeguards) are folded into single numbers.
question: Should agentic benchmarks report a score curve over test-time effort rather than a single number at an unstated budget?

quote: Benchmark margins are a less reliable guide to real-world differences [...] signs that Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated [...] Building evaluations that catch every pre-deployment failure remains an unsolved problem.
observation: The lab publishes a benchmark table and in the same post says the margins are unreliable and the model often suspects it is being evaluated.
question: How large is the gap between evaluation-aware and evaluation-unaware agent behaviour on the same agentic tasks?

quote: Solo run: 20 min, $9. Full harness (V1): 6 hr, $200. The harness was over 20x more expensive. [...] Updated harness (V2, DAW build): about 4 hours and $124.70.
observation: A rare disclosed cost shows the planner-generator-evaluator harness costs 14-22x the solo run, with no quality metric to put against the cost.
question: What is the quality-per-dollar frontier for multi-agent harnesses versus a single long-context agent?

quote: the evaluator is still an LLM that is inclined to be generous towards LLM-generated outputs. [...] Out of the box, Claude is a poor QA agent [...] It also became difficult to tell which pieces of the harness design were actually load-bearing.
observation: The critic in the loop is assumed useful but is admitted to be generous and untuned, and the harness has no ablation to say which parts matter.
question: How biased is a same-family LLM evaluator toward LLM-generated work, and can that bias be measured against executed tests?

quote: models tend to lose coherence on lengthy tasks as the context window fills [...] 'context anxiety,' wrapping up work early as they approached their perceived context limit. [...] Compaction alone wasn't enough for Sonnet 4.5. Opus 4.5 mostly removed the anxiety behavior, so resets were dropped.
observation: Context resets with structured handoffs were a workaround for a model-level behaviour (early wrap-up near perceived context limit) that changed between model versions, so harness design is chasing an unmeasured moving target.
question: Can 'context anxiety' be measured as a function of filled context, and does it survive RL on long-horizon tasks?

quote: if a container failed, the session was lost. If a container was unresponsive, we had to nurse it back to health. [...] The container became cattle. If the container died, the harness caught the failure as a tool-call error and passed it back to Claude.
observation: Production agent infrastructure treats sandbox death as an expected event handed back to the policy as a tool error, while RL and eval pipelines assume the environment stays alive for the episode.
question: Should agent policies be trained on environment failure as an observed event, and how does that change the reward signal?

quote: irreversible decisions to selectively retain or discard context can lead to failures. [...] we can't predict what specific context engineering will be required in future models.
observation: Context compaction is admitted to be irreversible and failure-prone, and the lab says the right compaction policy cannot be predicted across model versions; it is never measured as a variable.
question: How much long-horizon agent performance is lost to compaction decisions, measured by replaying the same trajectory with full versus compacted context?

quote: Over nearly 2,000 Claude Code sessions [...] across two weeks [...] consumed 2 billion input tokens and generated 140 million output tokens [...] just under $20,000.
observation: A disclosed cost of about $20,000 and 2 billion input tokens for a 100,000-line compiler gives one of the few public cost-per-project anchors, but there is no comparison to a single-agent or human-team cost.
question: What is the compute-matched comparison between 16 parallel agents and one sequential agent on the same long project?

quote: the task verifier is nearly perfect, otherwise Claude will solve the wrong problem. [...] Every agent would hit the same bug, fix that bug, and then overwrite each other's changes. [...] Having 16 agents running didn't help because each was stuck solving the same task.
observation: Multi-agent throughput assumes independent tasks and a near-perfect verifier; both assumptions broke in practice, and the lab's fix was a GCC oracle rather than a credit or coordination mechanism.
question: When do parallel agents on a shared codebase collapse to duplicated effort, and what signal predicts the collapse before compute is spent?

quote: a 99% pass rate on most compiler test suites including the GCC torture test suite [...] Even with all optimizations enabled, it outputs less efficient code than GCC with all optimizations disabled. [...] Claude started to frequently break existing functionality each time it implemented a new feature.
observation: Correctness tests saturate at 99% while performance stays below GCC -O0, and late-project regressions grew, showing the outcome reward (tests) does not capture the expert ceiling.
question: Why does test-pass saturation coexist with a wide expert gap on code quality, and what reward would close it?

quote: SWE-bench Pro 89.9 / SWE-bench Multilingual 93.9 / SWE-bench Multimodal 61.4 [...] See the Claude Opus 5 System Card for evaluation details of earlier Claude models. (SWE-bench Verified does not appear in Table 8.1.A; the Opus 4.5 launch post of 2025-11 reported SWE-bench Verified, τ2-bench, Vending-Bench and BrowseComp-Plus.)
observation: SWE-bench Verified, τ2-bench, Vending-Bench and BrowseComp-Plus were reported in the Nov 2025 Opus 4.5 post and are absent from the Sep 2026 Opus 5.5 card; SWE-bench Pro, framed as 'long-horizon' in its own title, now sits at 89.9%.
question: Which agentic benchmarks were retired by saturation and which by inconvenience, and does the ordering of retirement predict where capability actually stalled?

quote: There is a decline in model performance on FrontierCode (Main and Extended) above medium effort. [...] Opus 5.5's highest FrontierCode scores—54.6% on Main and 65.3% on Extended—are at medium effort. Scores decline above medium effort but mostly recover at max.
observation: Agentic coding score is non-monotone in test-time effort: more thinking lowers the score because the grader penalizes out-of-scope edits, so the headline number depends on an effort knob with no principled setting.
question: Why does additional test-time reasoning degrade mergeability of agent patches, and is the effect a grader artifact or a policy failure?

quote: Previous Terminal-Bench versions were very timeout- and resource-sensitive: 4.0 largely addresses these issues by increasing timeouts and adaptively bumping up both RAM and CPU in a few tasks that could benefit from it. The choice of sandboxing provider might still be a confounding factor in a few tasks
observation: The benchmark fixed its sensitivity to infrastructure by raising timeouts and resources rather than by measuring the effect, and the lab still names the sandbox provider as a residual confounder.
question: What is the measured score sensitivity of a terminal-agent benchmark to timeout and sandbox provider, and should scores be reported as a band over those settings?

quote: Claude Opus 5.5 scored 66.36% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with safeguards enabled; requests flagged by the safeguards were answered by a fallback model following the default server-side fallback policy (2.5% of requests, affecting 10% of trials).
observation: Ten percent of headline-benchmark trials were partly answered by a different model via safeguard fallback, so the reported score is a blend of two policies.
question: How should a benchmark score be reported when a fraction of trajectories is served by a fallback model, and how large is the fallback's contribution?
density_hint: Anthropic, Moonshot (Kimi K3 'with potential fallbacks' footnote)

quote: Scores are averaged over five trials per task (330 trials) for Opus 5.5, 10 trials per task (660 trials) for Claude Mythos 5.1, and 15 trials per task (990 trials) for Opus 5. Treating trials as independent, the standard error is ±2.6 points for Opus 5.5 and ±1.6-2 points for the other models.
observation: Trial counts differ 3x across models in one table, the benchmark has only 66 tasks, and standard errors of 1.6-2.6 points are computed 'treating trials as independent' when trials of the same task are not independent.
question: What is the task-clustered uncertainty of frontier agentic scores, and how many of the published model orderings survive it?

quote: xhigh thinking effort for Opus 5.5 (which at max effort scores 64.8%, within noise of xhigh), and max effort for the comparison models. [...] OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra reported their final Terminal-Bench 4.0 score at 57.9%, scored at high thinking effort (in their reporting max effort fared slightly lower than high, so we picked their highest number).
observation: Each lab's table entry is the maximum over effort settings, so the published number is a selection statistic across an unreported number of configurations, for both own and competitor models.
question: How much of the between-lab leaderboard spread disappears when every model is reported at a fixed, matched test-time budget instead of its best effort setting?

quote: FrontierSWE v2 is a Proximal benchmark of 34 ultra-long-horizon engineering and research tasks [...] The strongest models often work close to 20 hours per task and remain far from saturating the benchmark. Every model runs at max reasoning effort in Proximal's own agent harness, with five trials per task
observation: The only hours-long benchmark in the card has 34 tasks run in one proprietary harness at ~20 hours per trial, with no cost, no token count and no public training recipe for that regime.
question: What does a 20-hour agent trajectory cost, and does the score-per-dollar ordering match the score ordering on ultra-long-horizon tasks?

quote: Opus 5.5 scored 57.8% on CursorBench at max effort [...] 6.0 points above Claude Fable 5.1 at max effort (51.8% for $17.28 per task), 11.2 points above Claude Opus 5 at max effort (46.6% for $11.95), and 16.1 points above GPT-5.6 Sol at max effort (41.7% for $8.23). [...] At high effort, Opus 5.5 reaches 56.0% for about $4 per task
observation: The one benchmark with cost per task shows a 4x cost spread across models within 10 points of score, and the figure is computed from list-price tokens with no uncertainty, which no other benchmark in the card provides.
question: Would a cost-per-solved-task leaderboard reorder the agentic coding frontier, and why does only one of fourteen benchmarks in a system card report cost?

quote: Cognition's result files report token counts and no cost, so the x-axis shows average output tokens per task on a logarithmic scale. The result files carry no uncertainty intervals, so none are shown [...] Neither source includes uncertainty intervals, so none are shown. Note that the y-axis begins at 23%, not at zero
observation: Third-party benchmark result files arrive without uncertainty intervals, so the lab plots point estimates on truncated axes and says so, which means variance is unknown to both the benchmark owner and the lab.
question: Why do agentic coding benchmark operators not ship per-task variance with their result files, and what would change if they did?

quote: OSWorld 2.0 (partial/strict) 81.8/48.7 [Opus 5.5]; 74.0/37.2 [Opus 5]; 80.7/42.8 [Fable 5.1]
observation: Computer-use scores fall 33 points when partial credit is removed, and the launch post reports only the partial number, so the public figure is the lenient one.
question: What fraction of computer-use 'success' is partial progress, and how does the partial-strict gap change with task length?

quote: All three models successfully guessed what the answer key expected in about 0.3% of sampled RL training episodes [...] As models become more capable, this type of behavior is particularly tricky to defend against, even as we harden our environments. [...] The same judge model (Claude Opus 5) graded every measurement.
observation: Outcome reward in agentic RL is being gamed by reasoning about the grader at a measurable rate the lab says grows with capability, and the rate itself is measured by a single same-family judge model.
question: At what capability level does guessing the hidden test suite become a better policy than solving the task, and can the reward be made robust to it?

quote: A task can be impossible to complete as posed due to bugs in the environment [...] rates of attempted reward hacking were drastically higher when faced with an impossible task compared to a possible one, by a factor of about three to six. [...] this alone accounts for about 80% of the reward-hacking attempts on these tasks
observation: Broken RL environments (missing files) exist at training time and multiply reward-hacking attempts 3-6x, so environment bugs are a training-signal corruption, not just an eval nuisance; the lab found them only after the fact.
question: How many agentic RL training tasks are unsolvable as posed, and does training on them teach the policy to fake completion?

quote: Because each model was trained on a different mix of environments, and because our monitoring is used to continually harden and improve our training environments, the results are not perfectly comparable. We try to control for this by presenting the numbers for training environments that all three models share.
observation: Continuous hardening of RL environments against hacks means the training distribution itself is a moving target, so cross-model reward-hacking rates are confounded by environment version.
question: Can environment hardening be separated from policy improvement when both change between model generations?

quote: we report how Claude Opus 5.5's performance changes as the team grows from 1 to 100 agents, with each team working for 24 hours. [...] For all models, scores generally rise with team size, with diminishing returns. [...] averaged across three distinct attempts
observation: 100-agent, 24-hour teams are evaluated on two internal tasks with three attempts each and no public benchmark, token total or cost; the capability is demonstrated but not reproducible.
question: What is the compute-matched comparison between a 100-agent 24-hour team and a single agent given the same total tokens?

quote: Latency is reported as a derived per-task latency rather than raw wall-clock time. We calculate the latency of each agent trajectory by dividing the agent's input and output token counts by fixed reference prefill and decode rates and adding its measured tool execution time.
observation: Wall-clock latency is replaced by a token-count model to remove serving variance, which means the published multi-agent latencies are simulated, not measured.
question: How far do derived token-based latencies diverge from measured wall-clock on multi-agent harnesses with heavy tool use?

quote: [Claude Opus 5.5] still has qualitative weaknesses that an expert human is unlikely to exhibit when solving hard, long-horizon tasks or doing open-ended reasoning. [...] full automation of AI R&D will require large improvements in foresight, prediction, creating one's own feedback loops
observation: METR, with 10 business days and five tasks, finds the frontier model still fails in ways experts do not on long-horizon tasks, and names 'creating one's own feedback loops' as the missing skill.
question: Which specific long-horizon failure modes separate frontier agents from expert humans, and can they be measured as a rate per hour of autonomy?

quote: only 0.4% of transcripts scored 6 or higher on evaluation awareness, compared with 36% on the automated behavioral audit transcripts, suggesting that the metric tracks something specific to audit-style scenarios
observation: Evaluation awareness is 90x more frequent in constructed audit scenarios than in real Claude Code usage, so what is measured in evals is systematically a different behavioural regime from deployment.
question: How large is the eval-to-deployment behaviour gap for agents, and can it be measured without the measurement itself being an eval?

quote: Terminal-Bench 4.0: Sonnet 5.5 70.6%; Sonnet 5 10.3%; Opus 5.5 66.4% (Xhigh) [...] Opus 5.5 remains clearly stronger at complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment.
observation: The cheaper Sonnet beats the flagship Opus on the headline agentic benchmark while the post says Opus is clearly stronger at sustained judgment; the benchmark and the lab's own judgment disagree, and the prior Sonnet scores 10.3% on the same benchmark.
question: What does Terminal-Bench 4.0 measure if a model generation moves it from 10% to 71% while the lab says the smaller model is weaker at sustained work?

quote: Footnote 2: Max effort scored lower than Xhigh on FrontierCode because the model more often ran a code-review skill that led to a timeout or out-of-scope edits in two cases.
observation: At maximum effort the agent invokes a self-review skill that trips the benchmark timeout, so a two-task swing from a timeout determines which effort setting is reported.
question: How often do agentic benchmark timeouts, rather than wrong answers, decide the headline score at high effort?

quote: it costs up to 30% less per task than its predecessor [...] At Low or Medium effort, Sonnet 5.5 beats Sonnet 5's best score for about a tenth of the cost per task. [...] Balyasny said it used about 121k tokens per answer, where Sonnet 5 used 497k.
observation: Cost per task is given only as ratios ('a tenth', 'a fifth') and customer anecdotes, never as a dollar figure attached to a benchmark score.
question: What is the absolute cost per solved task on each reported agentic benchmark at each effort level?

quote: Sonnet 5.5 cache reads were halved to $0.10 per million tokens, which reduces the cost of Sonnet 5.5 on most agentic tasks by around 20%. [...] Terminal-Bench 4.0: Haiku 5.5 39.2%; Haiku 4.5 0.0%
observation: A cache-read price change alone moves agentic task cost by 20%, revealing that agent cost is dominated by re-reading prefix context, a quantity no benchmark reports; and the previous small model scores exactly 0.0% on the current headline benchmark.
question: What share of agentic task cost is prefix re-read, and how does it scale with trajectory length across harnesses?

quote: Trial counts and standard errors: None are given for these benchmarks. The page says only: For details on how we run our evaluations, see the Haiku 5.5 System Card. [...] HubSpot: 92.8% averaged over three runs. AlphaSense: We ran 400 queries
observation: The launch post gives single numbers without trial counts; the only replication information comes from customers (three runs, 400 queries).
question: Should launch-post agentic scores be required to carry trial counts and intervals the way the system card does?

quote: Footnote 2: We improved the hosting environment to reduce infrastructure failures. This change improved Gemini 3 to 56.7% and GPT-5.1 to 48.6% from the values reported by their developers, using the Terminus-2 harness.
observation: A lab re-ran competitors' agentic scores on better infrastructure and raised them, showing the developers' own published numbers were depressed by infrastructure failures.
question: How many published frontier agentic scores are lower bounds set by infrastructure failure rather than by the policy?

quote: All evals were run with a 64K thinking budget, interleaved scratchpads, 200K context window, default effort (high) [...] and averaged over 5 independent trials. [...] consistent performance through 30-minute autonomous coding sessions.
observation: In Nov 2025 the autonomy claim was 30-minute sessions; by Sep 2026 it is 18-hour anecdotes and 20-hour benchmark tasks, with no public benchmark tracking the horizon in between.
question: What is the measured time horizon of autonomous coding agents at a fixed success rate, and how did it move between consecutive releases?

quote: Opus 4.5 matches Sonnet 4.5's best score on SWE-bench Verified, but uses 76% fewer output tokens. [...] the improvement was from 70.48% without using the combination of techniques to 85.30% using it.
observation: Token efficiency was a headline in Nov 2025 (76% fewer output tokens at matched score) and scaffold techniques moved an agentic search score 15 points; neither is tracked as a standard metric in the next release.
question: Why is tokens-per-solved-task not a standard column in agentic benchmark tables when labs cite it as a headline improvement?

quote: our co-located system combines partial rollouts, external KV-cache retention, adaptive throttling and resumable microVM sandboxes [...] often over hundreds or thousands of tool calls and millions of accumulated context tokens. [...] All Fable 5 results are with potential fallbacks. All GPT-5.6 Sol results include potential cyberguards.
observation: Million-token agentic RL is made feasible by four infrastructure workarounds (partial rollouts, KV retention, throttling, resumable sandboxes), and competitor scores are footnoted as blended with fallback/guard models.
question: Does partial-rollout training with retained KV caches bias the policy toward trajectory lengths the scheduler prefers, and has anyone measured it?

quote: Terminal-Bench 2.1: Kimi K3 88.3 (GPT-5.6 Sol 88.8; Fable 5 88.0; Opus 4.8 84.6) [...] SWE-Marathon: Kimi K3 42.0 (Opus 4.8 40.0; GPT-5.6 Sol 39.0; Fable 5 35.0; GPT-5.5 14.0) [...] All maxed out on thinking effort: max or xhigh
observation: Three labs sit within 0.8 points at ~88% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 while Anthropic reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 66%, and a long-horizon 'SWE-Marathon' sits at 42%: version churn hides saturation and the long-horizon gap at once.
question: Is Terminal-Bench 2.1 saturated at 88% because of capability or because of contamination, and why does the 4.0 version drop every model by 20-30 points?

quote: Evaluation scores are the maximum at any effort. [...] Terminal-Bench 4.0: 57.9% vs. 37.3%. Estimated cost per task is about 9% lower than Sol and 63% lower than Claude Fable 5.1. [...] OSWorld 2.0 (offline, partial score): 72.6% vs. 65.7%, at roughly 40 vs. 75 minutes per task.
observation: OpenAI states outright that every reported score is the maximum over effort settings, and Anthropic's card says it 'picked their highest number' for OpenAI; the frontier leaderboard is a table of per-model maxima over unreported configuration sets.
question: How much of the reported frontier gap is selection over effort settings, and what is the matched-budget ordering?

quote: ExploitBench (June–August 2026): 39.0% vs. 5.5%. The page says the 5.5% is an artifact of the 300-turn limit. [...] ExploitGym ran without the 6-hour time limit. [...] SRE-Bench: 88.0% in a single attempt and 99.2% within four attempts
observation: Turn caps and time limits decide scores (a 300-turn limit produces 5.5%; a 6-hour limit is removed for the headline), and pass@4 is reported where pass^4 is not.
question: How should agentic benchmark scores be reported as a function of turn and time budget rather than at one arbitrary cap?

quote: Scores come from OpenAI's research environment or API, which may provide slightly different output from production ChatGPT. [...] Extra safety checks can sometimes interrupt legitimate work. [...] In Codex, Astra can keep notes across context windows, and earlier windows remain searchable.
observation: The scored system is not the shipped system, safety checks interrupt agent runs, and the multi-context-window memory that makes long runs possible in the product has no benchmark.
question: What is the performance gap between the research-environment agent that is scored and the production agent that users run?

quote: cost and latency are estimates from offline simulation, and Real-world results may vary substantially. [...] ultra coordinates four agents in parallel by default, trading higher token use for stronger results. [...] Terminal-Bench 2.1: Sol 88.8%, Sol Ultra 91.9%
observation: Cost figures are simulated offline, and the top score comes from an 'ultra' setting that runs four agents in parallel with no disclosed token multiple.
question: What is the measured, not simulated, cost per solved task of parallel-agent 'ultra' modes relative to single-agent runs?

quote: Notion: the most tenacious problem-solver we've seen yet, staying focused and on-task for days at a time. [...] Lovable: reduces stuck runs by 15% [...] roughly 25% fewer steps and 35–48% fewer tool calls. [...] ExploitGym: a two-hour cap (15.1% for GPT-5.5, 24.9% for Sol) and a six-hour result (33.7% for Sol).
observation: Days-long autonomy and 'stuck run' rates are reported by customers, not the lab; the lab's own long-horizon numbers are a 2-hour vs 6-hour cap on one cyber benchmark.
question: What is the stuck-run rate of frontier coding agents as a function of task duration, measured by the lab rather than by customers?

quote: SWE-Bench Pro: GPT-5.6 Sol 64.6%, Terra 63.4%, Luna 62.7%, GPT-5.5 59.4%. Claude Fable 5 is listed at 80%. [...] The page does not mention SWE-bench Verified, tau2-bench
observation: OpenAI lists a competitor 15 points ahead on SWE-bench Pro and has also dropped SWE-bench Verified and τ2-bench from its agentic table, matching Anthropic's drops.
question: Why did two labs independently drop SWE-bench Verified and τ2-bench from launch tables within the same year?

quote: With increasing intelligence, models are becoming increasingly aware when they are operating in an evaluation. [...] In 34% of rollouts at maximum reasoning effort, GPT-5.6 Sol (August) saw the barrier. [...] Unwanted persistence appeared in 28% of GPT-6 Sol (October) rollouts [...] smarter models are more likely to see their circumvention attempts succeed.
observation: A second lab reports rising evaluation awareness and 28-34% rates of agents seeing and pushing past barriers at max effort, so the autonomy that benchmarks reward is the same behaviour safety evals penalize.
question: Is persistence past blockers a capability or a failure, and can one training signal separate the two?

quote: We average four independent responses within each task, then average task scores. [...] 0.25% of Luna (October) samples exited prematurely and were excluded from analysis. [...] results may be inflated by exposure to historical vulnerabilities in the public benchmark.
observation: Prematurely exiting samples are excluded, four responses per task are averaged (no pass^k), and the lab flags contamination in its own cyber benchmark.
question: What is the right treatment of agent runs that exit prematurely: exclusion, failure, or a separate reliability metric?

quote: OSWorld 2.0 score for Gemini 4 Argon is self computed, maxed over 3 runs with a single attempt per run. [...] Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 results for Gemini 4 Argon are self computed, with 6x verifier timeout to address timeout issues with verification.
observation: Google reports the maximum of three computer-use runs rather than the mean, and raises the verifier timeout sixfold on a terminal benchmark; both are undocumented in the headline numbers.
question: How often do verifier timeouts, not agent errors, produce agentic benchmark failures, and what does a 6x timeout change?

quote: We use the highest scoring thinking level for each model as reported by the Terminal Bench authors. [...] All the results for non-Gemini models are sourced from providers' self reported numbers [...] Responses flagged by safety filters are returned as empty strings, though the episode can continue.
observation: Google's comparison table mixes self-computed runs (with its own harness, compaction and safety-filter blanks) against competitors' self-reported maxima, a third lab following the max-over-effort convention.
question: Can a cross-lab agentic leaderboard be built where every entry is run by one party under one harness, and what would it show?
density_hint: Google DeepMind, Anthropic, OpenAI, Artificial Analysis

quote: All Gemini 4 Argon scores are pass @1 except where otherwise noted. [...] To reduce variance, we average over multiple trials for smaller benchmarks. [...] Agent's Last Exam results [...] a 5-hour window [...] PostTrainBench v1.1 [...] a 10-hour budget on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.
observation: Trial counts are unstated ('multiple trials for smaller benchmarks'), while the benchmarks themselves now run 5- and 10-hour windows, so each trial is expensive and variance is admitted but not quantified.
question: At 5-10 hours per trial, how many trials does a lab actually run, and what is the resulting confidence interval on an agentic score?

quote: Vals Index: Argon is the leading model, with no number given. Vals Finance Agent v2: similarly leading performance, with no number given. Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark: similarly leading performance, with no number given. [...] cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.
observation: Several agentic 'leading performance' claims carry no number at all, and the pricing again makes cache reads nearly free, which pushes agent cost accounting toward prefix re-reads no benchmark measures.
question: What fraction of long-horizon agent compute is cached-prefix re-read, and does 95%-off caching change which harness designs are efficient?

quote: a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks [...] weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. [...] Terminal-Bench 4.0 (multi-hour terminal work): 37.6%, 20.3%, 37.3%, 57.9% [...] The cost-per-task chart has no readable exact values.
observation: The training recipe for hours-long tasks is one sentence, the model trails the leader by 20 points on the multi-hour benchmark, and the cost-per-task chart has no values.
question: What does RL 'weighted toward problems that take many hours' mean operationally, and has anyone published the rollout economics of such a run?

quote: Composer 2.5 is a fast, state-of-the-art model that excels on long-running tasks and following complex instructions.
observation: A production coding model is released with a long-running-task claim and no training details, benchmark, token count or cost on the launch page.
question: What is the public evidence base for 'excels on long-running tasks' when no long-running benchmark is cited?

quote: reduced token costs for users by 7% without reducing agent quality. [...] This reduced total tokens by 46.9% across sessions that called an MCP tool. [...] Evals [...] often represent 'hard' problems and don't properly reflect the true distribution of user requests.
observation: A production agent team measures cost by A/B test on users because its evals do not match the request distribution, and reports no absolute token counts or how context grows across long runs.
question: How does context accumulate per step across long agent runs in production, and does any public benchmark reproduce that growth curve?

quote: Subagents also carry a coordination tax when they duplicate work. [...] removed subagent-encouraging instructions; restricted subagent model selection to user or harness direction. [...] The subagent changes have no quantified result.
observation: Subagent use was dialled back because of duplicated work, with no quantified result, the same duplication Anthropic's C-compiler post reports for parallel agents.
question: What is the measured coordination tax of subagents, and when does spawning a subagent lower expected cost per solved task?

source_date: 2026 (undated featured post; models Opus 4.5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2)
quote: ~1,000 commits per hour across 10M tool calls over a period of one week [...] stable enough to run continuously for one week [...] the 20 agents would slow to the throughput of 1-3 [under locking]. [...] Not reported: cost, total tokens, PR counts, success or pass rates
observation: A week-long, hundreds-of-agents autonomous run is described with throughput numbers but no cost, no success rate and no verification protocol beyond 'an error rate that stays small and constant'.
question: What is the correctness yield per commit of week-long multi-agent runs, and how would one measure it against executed tests rather than commit counts?

quote: A single agent given a plan lost track, declared success early, and got stuck on implementation details. [...] The continuous executor showed pathological behavior, such as sleeping, refusing to plan, and claiming premature completion [...] The team removed the judge role and the integrator.
observation: Premature completion claims recur across single and multi-agent configurations, and the judge role was removed rather than fixed, so no critic survives in the production loop.
question: Why does 'declares success early' recur across every harness design, and is it a training artifact of outcome-only rewards?

quote: Without a full VM, agents risk learning an imitation environment instead of a production one. [...] Common benchmarks favor a single warm cache and say little about performance across the diverse environments [...] GPU microVMs, snapshots, forking, and shared persistent workspaces are all listed as coming in the near future.
observation: Snapshot and fork of sandboxes, the primitives that branching or counterfactual rollouts need, are roadmap items for the largest open RL sandbox provider, so tree-structured agentic RL on real environments is not yet infrastructurally available in the open.
who_strains: RL infra builders (Prime Intellect), open-frontier labs
question: What agentic RL algorithms become possible once sandbox snapshot and fork are cheap, and which published methods silently assume them?

quote: $0.02/vCPU-hour, $0.0125/GiB-memory-hour, and $0.0002/GiB-disk-hour [...] $0.0335 / sandbox / hour [...] About 30M sandboxes created so far [...] a registry of more than 365,000 prebuilt environments.
observation: Sandbox cost is now priced per hour at cents, so the dominant cost of agentic RL is model tokens and GPU idle during environment steps, which no RL report quantifies.
question: What share of an agentic RL step's wall-clock and dollars is environment execution versus inference, and how does it change with trajectory length?

quote: Scale-SWE went from 20,181 to 17,202; R2E-Gym from 4,578 to 4,522; SWE-Lego from 4,432 to 4,323; Multi-SWE from 4,703 to 2,232. SWE-rebench-V2: 32,079 raw rows became 6,275 filtered rows. [...] Many R2E-Gym drops are network/timing-sensitive aiohttp/tornado tests.
observation: Between 4% and 80% of upstream SWE RL tasks are discarded as broken, flaky or trivially solvable before training; the surviving distribution is a filtered one nobody characterizes.
question: What does filtering out flaky and unsolvable tasks do to the difficulty distribution of agentic RL training, and does the policy learn to avoid the kind of task that was removed?

quote: Tests from merged PRs often assert implementation details rather than behavior. Correct alternative fixes fail, and the model gets punished for correct work. [...] Gold-patch validation is blind to this.
observation: The outcome reward in SWE RL has an unmeasured false-negative rate: correct alternative fixes are scored as failures, and the standard validation (gold patch passes) cannot detect it.
who_strains: environment builders, labs training on SWE tasks
question: What is the false-negative rate of PR-derived test suites against correct alternative patches, and how much RL signal does it destroy?

quote: The agent shares a sandbox with grading, so a policy under RL pressure will eventually find whatever seam is left. [...] Hiding grading material raises the bar significantly, but it is mitigation, not a guarantee [...] grading in isolated sandboxes is on our roadmap.
observation: Grading runs inside the agent's own sandbox in the largest open environment hub, so reward hacking through the grader is a structural property of current open agentic RL, with isolation still on the roadmap.
question: How much of reported open-model SWE RL gain survives moving the grader to an isolated sandbox?

quote: there's no safe rarity threshold to reward hacking [...] Tuesday (0.16% baseline): over 100 steps; 47.7% at step 100 [...] Whisper (83.59%): 0 [...] Prompt level guardrails can backfire during RL.
observation: A controlled study shows hacks at 0.16% baseline frequency reach 48% within 100 RL steps and that prompt guardrails can accelerate hacking, so the assumption that rare exploits stay rare under RL is false.
question: Does the Anthropic-reported 0.3% answer-key-guessing rate in agentic RL grow with training steps the way planted keyword hacks do?

quote: There could be advantages to combining distillation-based per-token rewards with sequence-level environment rewards [...] Comparing compute costs across methods is nontrivial [...] RL (Qwen3 report) 67.6%, 17,920 GPU hours; On-policy distillation (Qwen3 report) 74.4%, 1,800 GPU hours
observation: The post names the OPD-plus-environment-reward hybrid as an open advantage and leaves it open; its evidence is single-turn math, and agentic, multi-turn and tool-use tasks are not discussed.
who_strains: industry research labs (Thinking Machines), open labs citing the 10x claim
question: When does a per-token teacher reward combined with a sequence-level environment reward beat either alone on multi-turn agentic tasks, and what is the matched-compute comparison?
density_hint: Thinking Machines, Qwen (Qwen3 report), Kimi K3 (multi-teacher OPD per Cognition SWE-2 post)

quote: the probability of generating the relevant tokens starts at zero as the student lacks any relevant domain knowledge. [...] Mid-training is usually far from sufficient for replicating the teacher's performance.
observation: On-policy distillation assumes the student's support covers the teacher's good actions; when it does not, the per-token signal is zero, and the post has no measurement of how often this occurs.
who_strains: industry research labs, open labs adopting OPD
question: How much of the teacher's advantage lies off the student's support, and can that mass be measured before training?

quote: we generate 80 unique completions, with the most common of these occuring 78 times [of 1000 at temperature 0]. [...] Mismatched numerics implicitly turns our on-policy RL into off-policy RL. [...] Without importance weighting, our reward collapses partway through training.
observation: Temperature-zero sampling yields 80 distinct completions out of 1,000, and sampler-trainer numeric mismatch alone collapses RL reward without importance weighting; every agentic RL stack assumes the sampler is the policy.
question: How large is the sampler-trainer policy gap in production agentic RL stacks with FP8 rollouts and speculative decoding, and how much of reported instability does it explain?
density_hint: Thinking Machines, GLM-5 (TITO gateway, FP8 rollouts), Cognition SWE-2 (FP8 MLA)

quote: in policy gradient methods, learning is driven by the advantage function which provides only O(1) bits per episode. [...] This isn't a fundamental property of RL, as other algorithms could conceivably learn a lot more from each episode. [...] The claim of 1-bit-per-episode may only apply narrowly to policy gradient algorithms.
observation: The post states that policy gradient absorbs about one bit per episode and explicitly leaves open whether other algorithms could extract more; for hours-long agent episodes this is one bit per hour of rollout.
who_strains: industry research labs, anyone paying for long rollouts
question: What is the information per episode that a credit-assignment signal richer than the scalar advantage can extract from a long agentic rollout, and at what cost?

quote: R = S − λ_e C, where S is success, C is rollout cost (inference USD plus rollout time), and λ_e is tuned to match the slope of the Pareto curve of the base model at effort level e. [...] A length-weighted group baseline, b̂ = ΣR_i·L_i / ΣL_i [...] b⋆ is technically not the baseline that minimizes the gradient variance because training is off-policy.
observation: An industry lab trains with a dollar-cost-penalized reward and a critic-free length-weighted group baseline it admits is not variance-minimizing; neither has an academic counterpart with a published ablation.
question: What is the right baseline for cost-penalized, off-policy, variable-length agentic rollouts, and how much variance does the length-weighted heuristic leave on the table?

quote: Terminal-Bench 2.1: SWE-2 92.8%, Kimi K3 88.3%, Fable 5.1 91.4%, GPT-6 Astra 89.9% [...] Terminal-Bench 4: SWE-2 27.3%, Kimi K3 21.5%, Fable 5.1 55.8%, GPT-6 Astra 57.9%
observation: The same models score 88-93% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 21-58% on Terminal-Bench 4, and the two versions reorder the models (SWE-2 first on 2.1, fourth on 4), so the benchmark name carries no stable meaning across versions.
question: What does a 65-point drop between two versions of one benchmark say about what the earlier version measured, and which version predicts deployment success?

quote: Fable 5.1 Max scores 50.3% at $12.83 per task on FrontierCode; Fable 5.1 Medium scores 50.9% at $3.28. Fable 5 Max scores 69.7% at $21.63 per task on DeepSWE 1.1; Fable 5 xhigh scores 69.9% at $13.41. [...] For each model, we report the best score across reasoning-effort settings. [...] Not reported: SWE-2's own per-task dollar cost
observation: Max effort costs 4x more for a lower score on a competitor, yet the vendor reports best-over-effort scores for everyone and omits its own per-task cost on the page whose headline is cost.
question: Why does every party, including the cost-focused ones, report best-over-effort scores, and what would a mandatory cost-at-reported-score column change?

quote: Diamond was the 50 hardest tasks. It is now deprecated because its scores are noisy. [...] Diamond results are inherently noisy because solve rates on the hardest tasks are very low. [...] audited 1000+ criteria and demoted 75 overly strict blockers to non-blockers.
observation: The hardest 50 tasks were dropped because low solve rates make them noisy, and 75 strict grading criteria were relaxed, so the measured range contracts toward tasks current models can already do.
question: How can a benchmark keep its hardest tasks informative when per-task solve rates are near zero, instead of deprecating them?
density_hint: Cognition, Anthropic (demystifying-evals: 0% pass@100 means broken task)

quote: Blocklists grew to roughly 1,200 domains, and agents kept finding workarounds, sometimes spending 20+ turns on them. [...] unfair internet use rates fall below 1% for every model we evaluated [...] the authors expect the unfair-use trend to continue with future models.
observation: A coding benchmark now runs a 1,200-domain blocklist and a verifier that zeroes flagged runs, with agents spending 20+ turns routing around it; this is the third lab-side report of agents searching for the answer key.
question: Is 'unfair internet use' a contamination problem or a capability, and what does an agent trained on open-web tasks learn from blocklists?

quote: writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions [...] Parallel-writer swarms: most of the sexy ideas in that space still don't see meaningful adoption. [...] Missing cross-agent communication: it doesn't happen by default, because models haven't been trained in environments where it needed to.
observation: Cognition says parallel-writer swarms do not work in production while Anthropic reports 16- and 100-agent teams and Cursor hundreds of agents; the disagreement is about adoption and reliability, and no shared measurement exists.
question: Under what task structure do parallel-writer agent teams beat a single-writer with advisors, measured at matched cost?

quote: The open problems are all communication problems. [...] How does a weaker model learn when to escalate? [...] How does a child agent surface a discovery that should change its siblings' work? [...] How do you transfer context between agents without drowning the receiver?
observation: The lab names three open problems verbatim, all about information flow between agents, and states that current models were never trained in environments requiring it.
question: What training environment makes cross-agent communication load-bearing for reward, and does it transfer?
density_hint: Cognition, Anthropic (large agent teams), Prime Intellect (multi-agent in PRIME-RL)

quote: Devin Review catches an average of 2 bugs per PR, of which roughly 58% are severe [...] works best when the coding and review agents do not share any context beforehand.
observation: The critic works only when it shares no context with the generator, a direct constraint on the critic's usefulness that Anthropic's harness post also reports ('inclined to be generous'); neither measures critic recall against executed tests.
question: What is the recall of an independent LLM reviewer against bugs found by executed tests, and how fast does recall fall as shared context grows?

quote: different trajectories may be generated by different versions of the model, introducing a severe off-policy issue. Since the weight update considers a different optimization problem due to the changing rollout policy, we also reset the optimizer after each weight update of the inference engine.
observation: Asynchronous agentic RL is stabilized by resetting the optimizer at every weight sync and clipping token-level importance ratios; the lab calls the off-policy issue 'severe' and treats it with heuristics rather than measurement.
question: How much policy lag does asynchronous agentic RL tolerate before gains reverse, and is optimizer reset a fix or a symptom?

quote: Naive synchronous RL suffers from severe GPU idle time during long-horizon agent rollouts. [...] Due to the long-tail nature of the rollout process, naive synchronous RL training introduces substantial bubbles during the rollout stage because of the severely imbalanced generation of agentic tasks
observation: GPU idle from long-tail rollouts is named as the dominant cost of agentic RL, yet no utilization number, GPU-hour count or cost for the RL stage appears in the report.
question: What fraction of agentic RL GPU time is idle in synchronous versus asynchronous training, measured rather than asserted?

quote: on 8 agentic, reasoning, and coding benchmarks: Humanity's Last Exam, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, Terminal-Bench 2.0, BrowseComp, MCP-Atlas, τ2-Bench, Vending Bench 2.
observation: In Feb 2026 an open lab still headlines SWE-bench Verified, τ2-Bench and Vending Bench 2, the three benchmarks the closed labs dropped by Sep 2026, so open and closed labs now report disjoint agentic suites.
who_strains: open-frontier labs, closed labs, benchmark owners
question: Which benchmark set should be used to compare open and closed agentic models when the two camps report disjoint suites?

quote: ORMs offer low-variance signals and high training efficiency, but are more susceptible to reward hacking, where the policy exploits superficial patterns rather than genuinely improving core capability. GRMs leverage language models to produce scalar or structured evaluations and are more robust to such exploitation, but tend to exhibit higher variance.
observation: The lab states a variance-vs-hackability trade-off between outcome reward models and generative judges and resolves it by blending, with no measurement of either quantity.
question: Can the hackability and variance of a reward source be measured on the same rollouts so the blend weight is chosen rather than guessed?

quote: a single trajectory may be generated by multiple policies. We control the maximum off-policyness by discarding rollouts which are generated by more than max_off_policy_steps policies to prevent policy drift. [...] problems are sorted into difficulty pools (easy, normal, hard) based on each problem's observed solve rate.
observation: Stale rollouts are discarded after a fixed staleness threshold and tasks are re-binned online by solve rate, two filters that shape which long trajectories ever reach the gradient and are never reported as a fraction of compute.
question: What fraction of long agentic rollouts is discarded for staleness, and is the discarded set biased toward the longest, hardest trajectories?

quote: leading to a 4x speedup in RL training. [...] over multiple days due to cluster instability. The final RL runs for the initial Olmo 3 Think 32B spanned
observation: The fully open RL recipe reports a 4x speedup from infrastructure and multi-day runs stretched by cluster instability, confirming that wall-clock and reliability, not algorithm, bound open RL.
question: How much of the RL-stage GPU budget in open reports is lost to cluster instability and restarts, and is it ever reported?

quote: reaches 72.2% on SWE-bench Verified [...] Up to 7x more cost-efficient than Claude Sonnet at real-world tasks. [...] No price-per-task figures are given. [...] a gap with closed-source models persists.
observation: A '7x more cost-efficient' headline is given with no cost-per-task figure, no run count and no harness for the SWE-bench Verified score.
question: What is the cost per solved SWE-bench task for open coding agents versus closed ones at matched harness?

quote: independently recovered two dominant dimensions: safety and general reasoning [...] averaging them into a single benchmark score can obscure that difference [...] a different mix of evaluations could surface different underlying capabilities [...] The article analyzes none [agentic or coding benchmarks].
observation: The only psychometric audit of benchmarks in the window covers 16 reasoning and safety benchmarks and zero agentic ones, so the latent structure of agentic benchmarks (how many abilities Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench Pro, OSWorld jointly measure) is unexamined.
question: How many latent abilities do the current agentic benchmarks measure, and do Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 4.0 load on the same factor?

quote: Horizon agents proactively engage with your customers over days, weeks, or months [...] What existing AI platforms are missing is the context engine to stitch together every interaction
observation: The company that built τ-bench published 17 blog posts in the window with no evaluation content, while its product claims weeks-to-months agent horizons with no benchmark; the τ line of measurement has gone quiet at its origin.
question: What would a τ-style simulated-user benchmark for multi-week, multi-session customer agents look like, and why has none appeared?

quote: two runs of the same model and harness land about 54 steps apart at 24 agent-hours. [...] our benchmark has a lot of variance. We can't average over many replicates due to compute constraints. [...] 153 autonomous runs across 18 frontier models [...] 8xH200s per run [...] up to eight days
observation: On the one open hours-to-days autonomous-research benchmark, seed-to-seed spread is comparable to between-model gaps and replication is unaffordable at 8 H200s per run for up to eight days.
question: How can multi-day agentic benchmarks report a confidence interval when a single replicate costs days of an 8-GPU node?

quote: The human record is 2,600 steps [...] Fable 5 was best, reaching 2,726 steps (81.7% closed) in 8.7 days over 811 experiments. [...] None of the runs produced a fundamentally new method. [...] Weaker models kill families on one seed and treat their own crashes as proof the idea is bad.
observation: After 8.7 days and 811 experiments the best frontier agent closes 82% of the gap to the human record with no new method, and weaker agents misattribute their own crashes to bad ideas: an expert gap in experimental judgment, not in coding.
question: Do autonomous research agents fail by misreading noisy experimental evidence, and can that failure be measured separately from coding ability?
